extracted.intended_audience: general early-18th-century readers and aspiring polite writers/poets (readers of The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional essay guidance on producing 'wit' and polished writing — diagnosing kinds of false wit, recommending readability and taste, and giving craft/process advice for poets and essayists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing a taste of polite writing
rubrics_metrics.description: As the great and only End of these Speculations is to banish Vice and Ignorance out of the Territories of Great-Britain, I shall endeavour as much as possible to establish among us a Taste of polite Writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing should refine public taste; critical commentary is justified when it tends to the 'Refinement and Perfection' of genres (operas, tragedies, comedy). The author frames criticism as civic and moral work, not mere decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and intelligibility to ordinary capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall endeavour to make what I say intelligible to ordinary Capacities; but if my Readers meet with any Paper that in some Parts of it may be a little out of their Reach, I would not have them discouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for accessibility: make prose understandable to ordinary readers. Permit occasional difficulty but balance it across installments (promise clearer follow-ups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate style for subject (avoid mismatch)
rubrics_metrics.description: I hope therefore I shall perform an acceptable Work ... that I may not incur the Censure which a famous Critick bestows upon one who had written a Treatise upon the Sublime in a low groveling Stile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match tone and register to subject: avoid lofty matters treated in a low style (and conversely avoid elevated diction in trivial contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false wit (general principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall trace out the History of false Wit, and distinguish the several Kinds of it ... a Writer does not show himself a Man of a beautiful Genius, but of great Industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False wit is contrivance and laborious artifice rather than genuine genius. Writers should avoid tricks that display industry at the expense of true intelligence and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shaped/figure poems (Scholar's Egg, Wings, Altar, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those short Poems printed among the minor Greek Poets, which resemble the Figure of an Egg, a Pair of Wings, an Ax, a Shepherd's Pipe, and an Altar ... the Author seems to have been more intent upon the Figure of his Poem, than upon the Sense of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make the shape the primary aim; when verse is cramped or stretched to fit a mould, sense and natural expression suffer. The author criticises poems whose form dominates content and calls this a venerable but false kind of wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let verse be crammed to fit artificial moulds
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poetry was to contract or dilate itself according to the Mould in which it was cast. In a word, the Verses were to be cramped or extended to the Dimensions of the Frame that was prepared for them; and to undergo the Fate of those Persons whom the Tyrant Procrustes used to lodge in his Iron Bed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid forcing language unnaturally (stretching or chopping lines) in order to make them fit a preordained visual or structural pattern; preserve organic expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid lipogrammatic gimmicks (letter-droppers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lipogrammiatists or Letter-droppers ... would take an Exception, without any Reason, against some particular Letter in the Alphabet, so as not to admit it once into a whole Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbitrary constraints that ban letters produce obsolete words, barbarisms, odd spellings, and awkwardness; they are a source of false wit and a 'treasury' of pedantry rather than poetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rebuses and picture-substitutions as mere conceits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rebus, that does not sink a Letter but a whole Word, by substituting a Picture in its Place ... Such a Device in so noble a Pile of Building looks like a Punn in an Heroick Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substituting pictures or devices for words (or using punny emblems) is often poor taste in elevated works; these conceits read as punning tricks and can blemish serious composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anthropomorphized mechanical devices (talking Echoes etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: I find likewise in ancient Times the Conceit of making an Eccho talk sensibly, and give rational Answers ... Hudibras ... ridicules this false kind of Wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devices like an Echo that answers with reasoned speech are silly and implausible; they typically mark weak invention and invite ridicule rather than admiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not revive antiquated or exploded modes of wit
rubrics_metrics.description: This I think the more necessary at present, because I observed there were Attempts on foot last Winter to revive some of those antiquated Modes of Wit that have been long exploded out of the Commonwealth of Letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of reviving obsolete fashions (shape-verses, rebuses, lipograms, mechanical conceits); their reappearance produces arrant blockheads pretending to polite authorship and degrades current taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value genius and natural invention over mere laborious ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: The Truth of it is, a Man had better be a Gally-Slave than a Wit, were one to gain that Title by those Elaborate Trifles which have been the Inventions of such Authors as were often Masters of great Learning but no Genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High labor and erudition cannot substitute for natural genius; avoid over-elaboration and contrived 'trifles' that demand endless pains but yield little true poetic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crafting and timing: devote focused time for comprehensive treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: I intend to lay aside a whole Week for this Undertaking, that the Scheme of my Thoughts may not be broken and interrupted; and I dare promise myself, if my Readers will give me a Week's Attention, that this great City will be very much changed for the better by next Saturday Night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating a complex subject like wit, organize and dedicate concentrated time to develop a thorough, coherent argument. Pace material so readers can follow and benefit from cumulative clarification.
